claim: Huntington's disease (HD) is a dominant inherited progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by expansion of a CAG repeat, coding a polyglutamine repeat within the N-terminal region of huntingtin protein.
source: Huntington's disease (HD) is a dominant inherited progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by expansion of a CAG repeat, coding a polyglutamine repeat within the N-terminal region of huntingtin protein (Macdonald, 1993; Vonsattel and DiFiglia, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Macdonald, 1993; Vonsattel and DiFiglia, 1998).

claim: Dysfunction and death of striatal medium-sized spiny neurons (MSSNs) is a key neuropathological hallmark of HD.
source: Although dysfunction and death of striatal medium-sized spiny neurons (MSSNs) is a key neuropathological hallmark of HD (Ferrante et al., 1991; Vonsattel et al., 1985), cognitive deficits appear long before the onset of motor disturbances (Lawrence et al., 2000; Lemiere et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ferrante et al., 1991; Vonsattel et al., 1985).

claim: Cognitive deficits appear long before the onset of motor disturbances in HD.
source: Although dysfunction and death of striatal medium-sized spiny neurons (MSSNs) is a key neuropathological hallmark of HD (Ferrante et al., 1991; Vonsattel et al., 1985), cognitive deficits appear long before the onset of motor disturbances (Lawrence et al., 2000; Lemiere et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Lawrence et al., 2000; Lemiere et al., 2004).

claim: Alterations in the dopaminergic system may contribute to HD neuropathology.
source: It has been postulated that alterations in the dopaminergic system may contribute to HD neuropathology (Chen et al., 2013a; Jakel and Maragos, 2000), as dopamine (DA) plays a key role in the control of coordinated movements.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2013a; Jakel and Maragos, 2000).

claim: Dopamine plays a key role in the control of coordinated movements.
source: It has been postulated that alterations in the dopaminergic system may contribute to HD neuropathology (Chen et al., 2013a; Jakel and Maragos, 2000), as dopamine (DA) plays a key role in the control of coordinated movements.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about dopamine's role in motor control.

claim: Increased DA levels and DA signaling occur at early stages of HD.
source: Increased DA levels and DA signaling occur at early stages of the disease (Chen et al., 2013a; Garret et al., 1992; Jakel and Maragos, 2000), resulting in an imbalance in striatal neurotransmission initiating signaling cascades that may contribute to striatal cell death (Paoletti et al., 2008; Ross and Tabrizi, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2013a; Garret et al., 1992; Jakel and Maragos, 2000).

claim: Increased DA levels and DA signaling result in an imbalance in striatal neurotransmission initiating signaling cascades that may contribute to striatal cell death.
source: Increased DA levels and DA signaling occur at early stages of the disease (Chen et al., 2013a; Garret et al., 1992; Jakel and Maragos, 2000), resulting in an imbalance in striatal neurotransmission initiating signaling cascades that may contribute to striatal cell death (Paoletti et al., 2008; Ross and Tabrizi, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Paoletti et al., 2008; Ross and Tabrizi, 2011).

claim: DA receptor antagonists and agents that decrease DA content reduce chorea and motor symptoms in HD.
source: Several studies demonstrated that DA receptor antagonists and agents that decrease DA content reduce chorea and motor symptoms while dopaminergic stimulation exacerbate such symptoms (Huntington Study Group, 2006; Mestre et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Huntington Study Group, 2006; Mestre et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2007).

claim: Dopaminergic stimulation exacerbates chorea and motor symptoms in HD.
source: Several studies demonstrated that DA receptor antagonists and agents that decrease DA content reduce chorea and motor symptoms while dopaminergic stimulation exacerbate such symptoms (Huntington Study Group, 2006; Mestre et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Huntington Study Group, 2006; Mestre et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2007).

claim: Two different MSSNs populations exist within the striatum: MSSNs expressing enkephalin and dopamine D2 receptors (D2R) giving rise to the indirect striatal efferent pathway, and MSSNs expressing substance P and dopamine D1 receptors (D1R) comprising the direct striatal efferent pathway.
source: Within the striatum, two different MSSNs populations can be distinguished: 1) MSSNs expressing enkephalin and dopamine D2 receptors (D2R), which give rise to the indirect striatal efferent pathway, and 2) MSSNs expressing substance P and dopamine D1 receptors (D1R), comprising the direct striatal efferent pathway.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about striatal neuron populations.

claim: D1R-MSSNs are more vulnerable to the HD mutation than D2R-MSSNs.
source: Recently, several studies with experimental models have changed the traditional view that D2R-MSSNs are more vulnerable in HD (Cepeda et al., 2008; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2007), proposing a new view in which D1R-MSSNs are more vulnerable to the HD mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cepeda et al., 2008; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2007).

claim: Mutant huntingtin enhances striatal cell death through the activation of D1R but not D2R.
source: In this view, it has been demonstrated that mutant huntingtin enhances striatal cell death through the activation of D1R but not D2R (Paoletti et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Paoletti et al., 2008).

claim: At early stages of HD, HD mice show an increase in glutamate release onto D1R neurons but not D2R neurons.
source: More recently, it has been described that, at early stages of the disease, HD mice show an increase in glutamate release onto D1R neurons but not D2R neurons while, later in the disease, glutamate release is selectively decreased to D1R cells (André et al., 2011a), indicating that several changes occur in D1R neurons at both early and late disease stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (André et al., 2011a).

claim: Later in HD, glutamate release is selectively decreased to D1R cells.
source: More recently, it has been described that, at early stages of the disease, HD mice show an increase in glutamate release onto D1R neurons but not D2R neurons while, later in the disease, glutamate release is selectively decreased to D1R cells (André et al., 2011a), indicating that several changes occur in D1R neurons at both early and late disease stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (André et al., 2011a).

claim: Strategies that might reduce D1R signaling could prove successful towards preventing HD.
source: Strategies that might reduce D1R signaling could prove successful towards preventing HD (André et al., 2011a; André et al., 2011b; Ross and Tabrizi, 2011; Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (André et al., 2011a; André et al., 2011b; Ross and Tabrizi, 2011; Tang et al., 2007).

claim: D1Rs are highly expressed in many tissues.
source: However, D1Rs are highly expressed in many tissues (Beaulieu and Gainetdinov, 2011) and broad use of D1R antagonists as a preventive treatment has important drawbacks including locomotor impairments (Giménez-Llort et al., 1997), or induce depression, parkinsonism and sedation in HD patients (Frank et al., 2008; Huntington Study Group, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Beaulieu and Gainetdinov, 2011).

claim: Broad use of D1R antagonists as a preventive treatment has important drawbacks including locomotor impairments.
source: However, D1Rs are highly expressed in many tissues (Beaulieu and Gainetdinov, 2011) and broad use of D1R antagonists as a preventive treatment has important drawbacks including locomotor impairments (Giménez-Llort et al., 1997), or induce depression, parkinsonism and sedation in HD patients (Frank et al., 2008; Huntington Study Group, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Giménez-Llort et al., 1997).

claim: D1R antagonists induce depression, parkinsonism and sedation in HD patients.
source: However, D1Rs are highly expressed in many tissues (Beaulieu and Gainetdinov, 2011) and broad use of D1R antagonists as a preventive treatment has important drawbacks including locomotor impairments (Giménez-Llort et al., 1997), or induce depression, parkinsonism and sedation in HD patients (Frank et al., 2008; Huntington Study Group, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Frank et al., 2008; Huntington Study Group, 2006).

claim: H3Rs are expressed in brain regions involved in both motor function (striatum) and cognition, such as the cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus and amygdala.
source: H3Rs are expressed in brain regions involved in both motor function (striatum) and cognition, such as the cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus and amygdala (Panula and Nuutinen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Panula and Nuutinen, 2013).

claim: In at least striatal GABAergic dynorphinergic neurons, both D1R and H3R are co-expressed.
source: It is known that in at least striatal GABAergic dynorphinergic neurons (Pillot et al., 2002; Ryu et al., 1994a; Ryu et al., 1994b), both D1R and H3R are co-expressed and we and others have found that they establish functional negative interactions by forming molecular complexes termed heteromers (Moreno et al., 2011; Sánchez-Lemus and Arias-Montaño, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pillot et al., 2002; Ryu et al., 1994a; Ryu et al., 1994b).

claim: D1R and H3R establish functional negative interactions by forming molecular complexes termed heteromers.
source: It is known that in at least striatal GABAergic dynorphinergic neurons (Pillot et al., 2002; Ryu et al., 1994a; Ryu et al., 1994b), both D1R and H3R are co-expressed and we and others have found that they establish functional negative interactions by forming molecular complexes termed heteromers (Moreno et al., 2011; Sánchez-Lemus and Arias-Montaño, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Moreno et al., 2011; Sánchez-Lemus and Arias-Montaño, 2004).

claim: D1R-H3R heteromers are expressed and functional in early HD stages but are lost in late stages.
source: Specifically, we demonstrate that D1R-H3R heteromers are expressed and functional in early HD stages but are lost in late stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including PLA and functional assays in HD mouse models at different ages.

claim: An H3R antagonist acting through D1R-H3R heteromers acts as a protective agent against dopaminergic imbalance in early HD stages.
source: An H3R antagonist acting through D1R-H3R heteromers acts as a protective agent against dopaminergic imbalance in early HD stages improving learning and long-term memory deficits and rescuing the loss of D1R-H3R complexes at late stages of HD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including behavioral assays and cell death assays in HD mouse models treated with thioperamide.

claim: An H3R antagonist improves learning and long-term memory deficits in early HD stages.
source: An H3R antagonist acting through D1R-H3R heteromers acts as a protective agent against dopaminergic imbalance in early HD stages improving learning and long-term memory deficits and rescuing the loss of D1R-H3R complexes at late stages of HD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including behavioral assays (rotarod, NORT, T-SAT) in HD mice treated with thioperamide.

claim: An H3R antagonist rescues the loss of D1R-H3R complexes at late stages of HD.
source: An H3R antagonist acting through D1R-H3R heteromers acts as a protective agent against dopaminergic imbalance in early HD stages improving learning and long-term memory deficits and rescuing the loss of D1R-H3R complexes at late stages of HD.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including PLA assays showing preserved heteromer expression in thioperamide-treated HD mice at 6 and 8 months.

claim: Both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells endogenously express similar levels of D1R and H3R.
source: Ligand binding determined that both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells endogenously express similar levels of D1R and H3R (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ligand binding data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: D1R-H3R heteromers were detected in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells by proximity ligation assays (PLA).
source: By proximity ligation assays (PLA), D1R-H3R heteromers were detected as red spots surrounding the blue stained nuclei in both cell types (Figure 1A, left panels of both cell types) and in cells treated with control lentivirus vector (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) but not in cells depleted of H3R (Figure 1A, right panels of both cell types) by shRNA, as shown by RT-PCR and functionality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), or in negative controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: D1R-H3R heteromers were not detected in cells depleted of H3R by shRNA.
source: By proximity ligation assays (PLA), D1R-H3R heteromers were detected as red spots surrounding the blue stained nuclei in both cell types (Figure 1A, left panels of both cell types) and in cells treated with control lentivirus vector (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) but not in cells depleted of H3R (Figure 1A, right panels of both cell types) by shRNA, as shown by RT-PCR and functionality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C), or in negative controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, along with RT-PCR and functional data confirming H3R depletion.

claim: The D1R agonist SKF 81297 increases ERK1/2 phosphorylation in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells.
source: Using both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells and concentrations of ligands previously shown to be optimal for receptor activation of the ERK1/2 pathway (Ferrada et al., 2009; Moreno et al., 2014; Moreno et al., 2011), we observed that the D1R agonist SKF 81297 was able to increase ERK1/2 phosphorylation whereas it was prevented by D1R antagonist SCH 23390, and by the H3R antagonist thioperamide (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B) via cross-antagonism.
evidence: The claim is supported by ERK1/2 phosphorylation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: ERK1/2 phosphorylation induced by SKF 81297 is prevented by D1R antagonist SCH 23390 in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells.
source: Using both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells and concentrations of ligands previously shown to be optimal for receptor activation of the ERK1/2 pathway (Ferrada et al., 2009; Moreno et al., 2014; Moreno et al., 2011), we observed that the D1R agonist SKF 81297 was able to increase ERK1/2 phosphorylation whereas it was prevented by D1R antagonist SCH 23390, and by the H3R antagonist thioperamide (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B) via cross-antagonism.
evidence: The claim is supported by ERK1/2 phosphorylation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: ERK1/2 phosphorylation induced by SKF 81297 is prevented by the H3R antagonist thioperamide via cross-antagonism in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells.
source: Using both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells and concentrations of ligands previously shown to be optimal for receptor activation of the ERK1/2 pathway (Ferrada et al., 2009; Moreno et al., 2014; Moreno et al., 2011), we observed that the D1R agonist SKF 81297 was able to increase ERK1/2 phosphorylation whereas it was prevented by D1R antagonist SCH 23390, and by the H3R antagonist thioperamide (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B) via cross-antagonism.
evidence: The claim is supported by ERK1/2 phosphorylation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Treatment with the D1R agonist SKF 81297 induces a robust and rapid increase in cytosolic Ca2+ in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells.
source: When cells were treated with the D1R agonist SKF 81297 a robust and rapid increase in cytosolic Ca2+ was detected in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium mobilization data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Calcium release induced by SKF 81297 can be dampened with the H3R antagonist thioperamide in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells.
source: Importantly, this calcium release could be dampened with the H3R antagonist thioperamide (cross-antagonism) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium mobilization data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: STHdh cell viability decreases when treated with the D1R agonist SKF 81297 in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: As expected, STHdh cell viability decreased when treated with the D1R agonist SKF 81297 in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Significant cell death in STHdh cells does not occur until 30 μM SKF 81297 is used.
source: Significant cell death did not occur until 30 μM SKF 81297 was used (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), an effect prevented by the D1R antagonist SCH 23390 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Cell death induced by 30 μM SKF 81297 is prevented by the D1R antagonist SCH 23390 in STHdh cells.
source: Significant cell death did not occur until 30 μM SKF 81297 was used (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), an effect prevented by the D1R antagonist SCH 23390 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Pre-treatment with the H3R antagonist thioperamide increases the number of surviving cells in the presence of the D1R agonist SKF 81297 in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells.
source: Pre-treatment with the H3R antagonist thioperamide, which did not modify cell viability when administered alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), increased the number of surviving cells in the presence of the D1R agonist SKF 81297 in both cell types (Figure 1L,M and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1L,M and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The H3R antagonist thioperamide does not modify cell viability when administered alone in STHdh cells.
source: Pre-treatment with the H3R antagonist thioperamide, which did not modify cell viability when administered alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), increased the number of surviving cells in the presence of the D1R agonist SKF 81297 in both cell types (Figure 1L,M and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: No protection from D1R agonist-induced cell death is observed in cells depleted of H3R with shRNA lentiviral infection.
source: Importantly, the effect of the H3R antagonist thioperamide was specific since no protection from D1R agonist-induced cell death was observed in cells depleted of H3R with shRNA lentiviral infection (Figure 1L,M), but was observed in cells transfected with the control lentivirus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1L,M.

claim: Protection from D1R agonist-induced cell death by thioperamide is observed in cells transfected with the control lentivirus.
source: Importantly, the effect of the H3R antagonist thioperamide was specific since no protection from D1R agonist-induced cell death was observed in cells depleted of H3R with shRNA lentiviral infection (Figure 1L,M), but was observed in cells transfected with the control lentivirus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Recovery of viability induced by the H3R antagonist thioperamide is mediated by D1R-H3R heteromers.
source: In addition, we also demonstrated that recovery of viability induced by the H3R antagonist thioperamide was mediated by D1R-H3R heteromers since pre-incubation with D1R TM5 peptide, but not D1R TM7 impaired the H3R antagonist protection from D1R agonist-induced cell death (Figure 1L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1L,M using interfering peptides.

claim: Pre-incubation with D1R TM5 peptide, but not D1R TM7, impairs the H3R antagonist protection from D1R agonist-induced cell death.
source: In addition, we also demonstrated that recovery of viability induced by the H3R antagonist thioperamide was mediated by D1R-H3R heteromers since pre-incubation with D1R TM5 peptide, but not D1R TM7 impaired the H3R antagonist protection from D1R agonist-induced cell death (Figure 1L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1L,M using interfering peptides.

claim: Both concentrations of the D1R agonist SKF 81297, cytotoxic (30 µM) and non-cytotoxic (1 µM), can induce intracellular calcium release, which is more pronounced and persistent at 30 μM.
source: Both concentrations of the D1R agonist SKF 81297, cytotoxic (30 µM) and non-cytotoxic (1 µM), can induce intracellular calcium release, which is more pronounced and persistent at 30 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium mobilization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Increased phosphorylation of p38 only occurs at the cytotoxic concentration (30 μM) of SKF 81297.
source: Interestingly, we found that increased phosphorylation of p38 only occurred at the cytotoxic concentration of SKF 81297.
evidence: The claim is supported by p38 phosphorylation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: The calcium release induced by 30 μM SKF 81297 is blocked by the H3R antagonist thioperamide.
source: Similar to treatment with 1 μM SKF 81297 (see Figure 1), the calcium release induced by 30 μM SKF 81297 was also blocked by the H3R antagonist thioperamide (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium mobilization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: Treatment with the H3R antagonist thioperamide reduces p38 phosphorylation upon D1R activation in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells.
source: Treatment with the H3R antagonist thioperamide reduced p38 phosphorylation upon D1R activation in both cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by p38 phosphorylation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The p38 inhibitor SB 203580 blocks p38 phosphorylation in STHdh cells.
source: Moreover, the p38 inhibitor SB 203580 blocked p38 phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C) and protected against the cytotoxic effect of the D1R agonist SKF 81297 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D), confirming that p38 is a key pathway involved in D1R-mediated cell death in these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by p38 phosphorylation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The p38 inhibitor SB 203580 protects against the cytotoxic effect of the D1R agonist SKF 81297 in a dose-dependent manner in STHdh cells.
source: Moreover, the p38 inhibitor SB 203580 blocked p38 phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C) and protected against the cytotoxic effect of the D1R agonist SKF 81297 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D), confirming that p38 is a key pathway involved in D1R-mediated cell death in these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: p38 is a key pathway involved in D1R-mediated cell death in STHdh cells.
source: Moreover, the p38 inhibitor SB 203580 blocked p38 phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C) and protected against the cytotoxic effect of the D1R agonist SKF 81297 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D), confirming that p38 is a key pathway involved in D1R-mediated cell death in these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that p38 inhibition blocks SKF 81297-induced cell death.

claim: SKF 81297 induces a loss of PLA staining in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells.
source: We found that SKF 81297-induced a loss of PLA staining in both STHdh cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), while pre-treatment with the H3R antagonist thioperamide preserved the number of punctate PLA spots (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Pre-treatment with the H3R antagonist thioperamide preserves the number of punctate PLA spots in both STHdhQ7 and STHdhQ111 cells.
source: We found that SKF 81297-induced a loss of PLA staining in both STHdh cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), while pre-treatment with the H3R antagonist thioperamide preserved the number of punctate PLA spots (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Both HdhQ7/Q7 and HdhQ7/Q111 mice display D1R-H3R heteromers at 2 months and 4 months of age in striatum, cerebral cortex and hippocampus.
source: By PLA we confirmed that both HdhQ7/Q7 and HdhQ7/Q111 mice display D1R-H3R heteromers at 2 months (mo) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and four mo (Figure 2A,B) of age in all brain regions tested.
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2A,B.

claim: Heteromer expression is similar in all brain areas and no differences are observed between HdhQ7/Q7 and HdhQ7/Q111 genotypes at 4 months of age.
source: Heteromer expression was similar in all brain areas and no differences were observed between genotypes at 4 mo of age (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA quantification data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: An almost complete loss of D1R-H3R heteromers is found in 6 month and 8 month-old HdhQ7/Q111 mice but not in HdhQ7/Q7 mice.
source: Surprisingly, an almost complete loss of D1R-H3R heteromers was found in 6 mo and eight mo-old HdhQ7/Q111 mice but not in HdhQ7/Q7 mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3A,B), indicating that at more advanced disease stages the D1R-H3R heteromer is lost.
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3A,B.

claim: At 8 months of age, a partial decrease in striatal D1R expression is detected in HdhQ7/Q111 compared with HdhQ7/Q7 mice using ligand binding experiments.
source: Although at 8 mo of age we detected a partial decrease in striatal D1R expression in HdhQ7/Q111 compared with HdhQ7/Q7 mice using ligand binding experiments (Supplementary file 2), the loss of heteromer expression is not due to a complete loss of receptor expression since by radioligand binding (Supplementary file 2) and mRNA expression analysis (Supplementary file 3) both receptors continue to be expressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by ligand binding data presented in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The loss of heteromer expression is not due to a complete loss of receptor expression since both D1R and H3R continue to be expressed at 8 months.
source: Although at 8 mo of age we detected a partial decrease in striatal D1R expression in HdhQ7/Q111 compared with HdhQ7/Q7 mice using ligand binding experiments (Supplementary file 2), the loss of heteromer expression is not due to a complete loss of receptor expression since by radioligand binding (Supplementary file 2) and mRNA expression analysis (Supplementary file 3) both receptors continue to be expressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by radioligand binding data (Supplementary file 2) and mRNA expression data (Supplementary file 3).

claim: D1R agonist SKF 81297 treatment increases the percentage of cell death in striatal, cortical and hippocampal organotypic cultures from 4-month-old HdhQ7/Q7 and HdhQ7/Q111 mice without significant differences between genotypes.
source: As expected, D1R agonist SKF 81297 treatment increased the percentage of cell death in all three regions compared to vehicle-treated organotypic cultures without significant differences between genotypes at 4 mo of age (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell death data in organotypic cultures shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Slices pre-treated with the H3R antagonist thioperamide protect cells from D1R elicited cell death in an equivalent manner to the D1R antagonist SCH 23390 in 4-month-old HdhQ7/Q7 and HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
source: Importantly, slices pre-treated with the H3R antagonist thioperamide, that does not modify cell death when administered alone, protected cells from D1R elicited cell death in an equivalent manner to the D1R antagonist SCH 23390 (Figure 2C), indicating that functional D1R-H3R heteromers are expressed in different brain areas of HdhQ7/Q7 and HdhQ7/Q111 mice at early disease stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell death data in organotypic cultures shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The H3R antagonist thioperamide does not modify cell death when administered alone in organotypic cultures.
source: Importantly, slices pre-treated with the H3R antagonist thioperamide, that does not modify cell death when administered alone, protected cells from D1R elicited cell death in an equivalent manner to the D1R antagonist SCH 23390 (Figure 2C), indicating that functional D1R-H3R heteromers are expressed in different brain areas of HdhQ7/Q7 and HdhQ7/Q111 mice at early disease stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell death data in organotypic cultures shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Functional D1R-H3R heteromers are expressed in different brain areas of HdhQ7/Q7 and HdhQ7/Q111 mice at early disease stages.
source: Importantly, slices pre-treated with the H3R antagonist thioperamide, that does not modify cell death when administered alone, protected cells from D1R elicited cell death in an equivalent manner to the D1R antagonist SCH 23390 (Figure 2C), indicating that functional D1R-H3R heteromers are expressed in different brain areas of HdhQ7/Q7 and HdhQ7/Q111 mice at early disease stages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that thioperamide protects against D1R-induced cell death in organotypic cultures from 4-month-old mice.

claim: The lack of protection of the H3R antagonist thioperamide against SKF 81297-induced cell death in organotypic cultures from 8-month-old HdhQ7/Q111 mice corroborates that the presence of D1R-H3R heteromers is needed for the H3R antagonist to prevent D1R-mediated cell death.
source: The dramatic change in heteromer expression in eight mo-old HdhQ7/Q111 mice was mirrored by the lack of protection of the H3R antagonist thioperamide against SKF 81297-induced cell death in organotypic cultures (Figure 3C), corroborating that the presence of D1R-H3R heteromers is needed for the H3R antagonist to prevent D1R-mediated cell death.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell death data in organotypic cultures shown in Figure 3C, correlated with the loss of heteromer expression.

claim: Cognitive decline is observed in HdhQ7/Q111 mice from 6 months of age.
source: Since cognitive decline is observed in these HD mice from 6 mo of age (Brito et al., 2014; Giralt et al., 2012; Puigdellívol et al., 2015) and the D1R-H3R heteromers are expressed and functional until the age of 5 mo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), we chose 5mo-old animals to start the thioperamide treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brito et al., 2014; Giralt et al., 2012; Puigdellívol et al., 2015).

claim: D1R-H3R heteromers are expressed and functional until the age of 5 months in HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
source: Since cognitive decline is observed in these HD mice from 6 mo of age (Brito et al., 2014; Giralt et al., 2012; Puigdellívol et al., 2015) and the D1R-H3R heteromers are expressed and functional until the age of 5 mo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), we chose 5mo-old animals to start the thioperamide treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA and functional data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Saline-treated mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice are unable to maintain their balance on the rotarod as wild-type HdhQ7/Q7 mice, revealing impaired acquisition of new motor skills.
source: Saline-treated mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice were unable to maintain their balance on the rotarod as wild-type HdhQ7/Q7 mice revealing impaired acquisition of new motor skills (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by rotarod behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Chronic treatment with thioperamide completely rescues motor learning deficits in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
source: Chronic treatment with thioperamide completely rescued motor learning deficits in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice as evidenced by a similar latency to fall in the accelerating rotarod as wild-type HdhQ7/Q7 mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by rotarod behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Saline-treated HdhQ7/Q111 mice do not show any preference for the novel object with respect to the familiar one in the NORT, indicating recognition LTM deficits.
source: Whereas saline-treated HdhQ7/Q111 mice did not show any preference for the novel object with respect to the familiar one, indicating recognition LTM deficits, thioperamide treatment completely prevented this LTM deficit in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by NORT behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Thioperamide treatment completely prevents recognition LTM deficits in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
source: Whereas saline-treated HdhQ7/Q111 mice did not show any preference for the novel object with respect to the familiar one, indicating recognition LTM deficits, thioperamide treatment completely prevented this LTM deficit in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by NORT behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Saline-treated HdhQ7/Q111 mice have no preferences between the novel arm and the old arm in the T-SAT, indicating spatial LTM deficits.
source: After 5 hr, a testing session showed that saline-treated HdhQ7/Q111 mice had no preferences between the novel arm and the old arm, indicating spatial LTM deficits (Figure 4C, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by T-SAT behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice treated with thioperamide spend more time in the novel versus the old arm in the T-SAT, revealing preserved LTM.
source: Interestingly, mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice treated with thioperamide spent more time in the novel versus the old arm, revealing preserved LTM (Figure 4C, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by T-SAT behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Thioperamide treatment is effective in restoring motor learning and preventing spatial and recognition LTM deficits in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate the effectiveness of thioperamide treatment in restoring motor learning and preventing spatial and recognition LTM deficits in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
evidence: The claim is a summary of behavioral data from rotarod, NORT, and T-SAT experiments.

claim: In saline-treated 6-month-old HdhQ7/Q111 mice, heteromer expression is significantly diminished with respect to age-matched HdhQ7/Q7 mice.
source: By PLA we observed that in saline-treated 6-mo-old HdhQ7/Q111 mice the heteromer expression was significantly diminished with respect to the age-matched HdhQ7/Q7 mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Treatment with thioperamide significantly prevents the loss of D1R-H3R heteromers in all brain regions analyzed in HdhQ7/Q111 mice at both 6 and 8 months of age.
source: Notably, treatment with thioperamide significantly prevented the loss of D1R-H3R heteromers in all brain regions analyzed in HdhQ7/Q111 mice at both 6 (Figure 4D,E) and 8 mo of age (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: A significant decrease in dendritic spine density in the hippocampus and the motor cortex of mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice has been described without significant alterations in the striatum.
source: We recently described a significant decrease in dendritic spine density in the hippocampus (Brito et al., 2014) and the motor cortex of mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice (Puigdellívol et al., 2015) without significant alterations in the striatum.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Brito et al., 2014; Puigdellívol et al., 2015).

claim: A significant reduction in the density of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta is found in the stratum radiatum and stratum oriens of saline-treated 6-month-old mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice compared to saline-treated wild-type HdhQ7/Q7 mice.
source: Confocal microscopy analyses revealed a significant reduction in the density of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta in the stratum radiatum (apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons) and stratum oriens (basal dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons) of saline-treated 6-mo-old mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice compared to saline-treated wild-type HdhQ7/Q7 mice (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by spinophilin immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Thioperamide treatment prevents the decline in the number of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta in the hippocampus of mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
source: Interestingly, thioperamide treatment prevented the decline in the number of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by spinophilin immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A significant reduction in the density of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta is found in layer I and layer II-III, but not layer V, of the motor cortex of 6-month-old saline-treated HdhQ7/Q111 mice compared to saline-treated HdhQ7/Q7 mice.
source: A significant reduction in the density of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta in layer I and layer II-III, but not layer V, of the motor cortex of 6-mo-old saline-treated HdhQ7/Q111 mice was found compared to saline-treated HdhQ7/Q7 mice (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by spinophilin immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Thioperamide-treated HdhQ7/Q111 mice exhibit a complete recovery in the density of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta in the motor cortex.
source: Interestingly, thioperamide-treated HdhQ7/Q111 mice exhibited a complete recovery in the density of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by spinophilin immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No significant differences are found between groups when the mean size of spinophilin puncta is analyzed.
source: No significant differences were found between groups when the mean size of spinophilin puncta was analyzed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by spinophilin puncta size analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The loss of spinophilin immunoreactive-puncta in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice can be ameliorated by thioperamide treatment.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that the loss of spinophilin immunoreactive-puncta in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice can be ameliorated by thioperamide treatment.
evidence: The claim is a summary of spinophilin immunostaining data.

claim: Thioperamide treatment fails to prevent the accumulation of mhtt oligomeric forms in HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
source: Thioperamide treatment failed to prevent the accumulation of these oligomeric forms (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No significant differences between groups are found when soluble monomeric mhtt levels are analyzed.
source: No significant differences between groups were found when soluble monomeric mhtt levels were analyzed (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Saline-treated HdhQ7/Q111 mice at 8 months exhibit poor performance in the accelerating rotarod task showing shorter latency to fall compared to wild-type HdhQ7/Q7 mice.
source: As expected, saline-HdhQ7/Q111 mice exhibited poor performance in this task showing shorter latency to fall compared to wild-type HdhQ7/Q7 mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by rotarod behavioral data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Thioperamide treatment starting at 7 months has no effect on motor learning performance in HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
source: Notably, thioperamide treatment had no effect on motor learning performance as both saline- and thioperamide-treated mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice were indistinguishable demonstrated by similar latency to fall in the accelerating rotarod task (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by rotarod behavioral data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Saline-treated 8-month-old HdhQ7/Q111 mice exhibit long-term memory deficits when recognition memory is analyzed using the NORT.
source: Saline-treated 8-mo-old HdhQ7/Q111 mice exhibited long-term memory deficits when recognition memory was analyzed using the novel object recognition test (NORT) (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by NORT behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Chronic treatment with thioperamide starting at 7 months does not rescue HdhQ7/Q111 mice from memory deficits.
source: Similar to motor learning results, chronic treatment with thioperamide did not rescue HdhQ7/Q111 mice from memory deficits (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by NORT behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The effect of thioperamide in learning and memory in HdhQ7/Q111 mice requires the proper expression and function of D1R-H3R heteromers.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that the effect of thioperamide in learning and memory in HdhQ7/Q111 mice requires the proper expression and function of D1R-H3R heteromers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that thioperamide is ineffective when treatment starts at 7 months, when heteromers are lost.

claim: The loss of heteromer expression compared with wild-type littermates is observed in R6/1 and R6/2 transgenic HD mouse models.
source: The loss of heteromer expression compared with wild-type littermates was also observed in other mouse models of HD, the R6/1 and R6/2 mice transgenic for the human huntingtin exon 1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: D1R-H3R heteromers are detected in human caudate-putamen slices from control individuals and low-grade (grade 0, 1 and 2) HD patients.
source: Importantly, D1R-H3R heteromers were detected as green spots surrounding the blue stained nuclei in human caudate-putamen slices from control individuals and low-grade (grade 0, 1 and 2) HD patients (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data in human brain slices shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Green spots are almost absent in samples from high-grade (grade 3 or grade 4) HD patients.
source: In contrast, green spots were almost absent in samples from high-grade (grade 3 or grade 4) HD patients (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data in human brain slices shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: D1R-H3R heteromer formation changes during HD disease progression.
source: These results show that D1R-H3R heteromer formation changes during disease progression and, importantly, that humans express D1R-H3R heteromers at early disease stages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from PLA data showing heteromers in low-grade but not high-grade HD patients.

claim: Humans express D1R-H3R heteromers at early disease stages.
source: These results show that D1R-H3R heteromer formation changes during disease progression and, importantly, that humans express D1R-H3R heteromers at early disease stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data in human brain slices from control and low-grade HD patients.

claim: Excess dopamine signaling via D1R leads to cell death by activating the p38 pathway.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that 1) excess dopamine signaling via D1R leads to cell death by activating the p38 pathway; 2) D1R-H3R complexes are found within the striatum, cortex and hippocampus of WT mice and in HD mice at early but not late disease stages; 3) targeting D1R via D1R-H3R complexes can slow progression of the disease in early but not late stages when the complexes are lost; and 4) D1R-H3R complexes are expressed in the human brain and thus represent potential therapeutic targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that D1R activation induces p38 phosphorylation and cell death, and that p38 inhibition blocks cell death.

claim: D1R-H3R complexes are found within the striatum, cortex and hippocampus of WT mice and in HD mice at early but not late disease stages.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that 1) excess dopamine signaling via D1R leads to cell death by activating the p38 pathway; 2) D1R-H3R complexes are found within the striatum, cortex and hippocampus of WT mice and in HD mice at early but not late disease stages; 3) targeting D1R via D1R-H3R complexes can slow progression of the disease in early but not late stages when the complexes are lost; and 4) D1R-H3R complexes are expressed in the human brain and thus represent potential therapeutic targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data showing heteromers in multiple brain regions at 2 and 4 months but not at 6 and 8 months in HD mice.

claim: Targeting D1R via D1R-H3R complexes can slow progression of the disease in early but not late stages when the complexes are lost.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that 1) excess dopamine signaling via D1R leads to cell death by activating the p38 pathway; 2) D1R-H3R complexes are found within the striatum, cortex and hippocampus of WT mice and in HD mice at early but not late disease stages; 3) targeting D1R via D1R-H3R complexes can slow progression of the disease in early but not late stages when the complexes are lost; and 4) D1R-H3R complexes are expressed in the human brain and thus represent potential therapeutic targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral and neuropathological data showing that thioperamide is effective when treatment starts at 5 months but not at 7 months.

claim: D1R-H3R complexes are expressed in the human brain and represent potential therapeutic targets.
source: In the present study, we demonstrate that 1) excess dopamine signaling via D1R leads to cell death by activating the p38 pathway; 2) D1R-H3R complexes are found within the striatum, cortex and hippocampus of WT mice and in HD mice at early but not late disease stages; 3) targeting D1R via D1R-H3R complexes can slow progression of the disease in early but not late stages when the complexes are lost; and 4) D1R-H3R complexes are expressed in the human brain and thus represent potential therapeutic targets.
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data showing heteromers in human brain slices from control and low-grade HD patients.

claim: This is the first demonstration of GPCR heteromers as potential targets to treat HD.
source: This is the first demonstration of GPCR heteromers as potential targets to treat HD.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings in the context of HD research.

claim: D1R is a major executor of the final signaling cascades that lead to cell death in HD.
source: Although we cannot rule out the participation of D2R in striatal degeneration, our results suggest that D1R is a major executor of the final signaling cascades that lead to cell death in HD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that D1R activation leads to cell death and that blocking D1R signaling is protective.

claim: D1R is in excess over D2R in the striatum.
source: This is further supported by the fact that D1R is in excess over D2R in the striatum, so it is plausible that the former will be more significantly activated than the latter at increased DA levels.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about receptor expression in the striatum.

claim: A toxic but not sub-toxic concentration of SKF81297 activates the p38 pro-apoptotic pathway.
source: We have demonstrated that a toxic but not sub-toxic concentration of SKF81297 activates the p38 pro-apoptotic pathway, despite both concentrations triggering calcium release, albeit at different levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing p38 phosphorylation only at 30 μM SKF 81297.

claim: p38 inhibitors completely abrogate the cell death induced by SKF81297 treatment.
source: Accordingly, p38 inhibitors completely abrogated the cell death induced by SKF81297 treatment, supporting the benefits of modulation of D1R signaling as potential treatment in HD.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability data showing that SB 203580 protects against SKF 81297-induced cell death.

claim: Direct manipulation of DA production and/or D1R signalling via a specific antagonist has limited therapeutic ability due to associated deleterious side effects.
source: However, direct manipulation of DA production and/or D1R signalling via a specific antagonist has limited therapeutic ability due to associated deleterious side effects.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the limitations of D1R antagonists.

claim: An interaction between H3R and the dopaminergic system has been previously reported.
source: An interaction between H3R and the dopaminergic system has been previously reported by us and others (Kononoff Vanhanen et al., 2016; Rapanelli et al., 2016; Rapanelli et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kononoff Vanhanen et al., 2016; Rapanelli et al., 2016; Rapanelli et al., 2014).

claim: H3R ligands completely abrogate striatal cell death induced by D1R, likely by inhibition of D1R-mediated calcium influx and p38 activation.
source: In this frame, we have demonstrated that H3R ligands completely abrogate striatal cell death induced by D1R, likely by inhibition of D1R-mediated calcium influx and p38 activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that thioperamide blocks D1R-induced calcium release, p38 phosphorylation, and cell death.

claim: The efficacy of the disrupting peptides supports protein-protein-driven effects in D1R-H3R heteromers.
source: The mechanisms of action of D1R-H3R heteromers can be multiple including allosteric effects. Indeed, the efficacy of the disrupting peptides supports protein-protein-driven effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that TM5 peptide disrupts heteromers and blocks thioperamide's effects.

claim: Heteromer formation may alter the trafficking of D1R, which could have pleiotropic consequences on signaling.
source: A second and potentially additional mechanism is that heteromer formation may alter the trafficking of D1R, which could have pleiotropic consequences on signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: Overstimulation of D1R induces receptor internalization promoting rapid intracellular signaling.
source: For example it is known that overstimulation of D1R induces receptor internalization promoting rapid intracellular signaling (Kotowski et al., 2011) and that receptor internalization can activate secondary signaling pathways (Lohse and Calebiro, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kotowski et al., 2011; Lohse and Calebiro, 2013).

claim: Thioperamide treatment maintains the PLA signal in vitro.
source: We observe in vitro that thioperamide treatment maintains the PLA signal while in vivo we see similar effects.
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data showing preserved heteromers after thioperamide treatment.

claim: D1R-H3R heteromers are stable enough to affect both rapid receptor signaling (e.g., Ca2+ mobilization) and longer cell signaling pathways like p38.
source: For the case of D1R-H3R heteromers, it appears that they are stable enough that they can affect both rapid receptor signaling (e.g., Ca2+ mobilization) and longer cell signaling pathways like p38, two events that have previously been involved in neuronal cell death in HD (Dau et al., 2014; Fan et al., 2012; Muller and Leavitt, 2014; Taylor et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that heteromers affect both calcium signaling and p38 phosphorylation.

claim: It is unclear what controls D1R-H3R heteromer formation or why it is lost during progression of HD.
source: It is unclear what controls D1R-H3R heteromer formation or why it is lost during progression of HD.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study.

claim: H3R ligands by targeting D2R-H3R heteromers could block D2R signaling and contribute to cell death protection.
source: Our findings do not rule out that H3R ligands by targeting D2R-H3R heteromers (Ferrada et al., 2008) could block D2R signaling and contribute to cell death protection.
evidence: This is a speculative claim acknowledging alternative mechanisms.

claim: D1R over-activation induces cell death-related pathways and D1R-H3R disruption.
source: However, several findings argue in favor of D1R-H3R heteromer as uniquely responsible for the effects of thioperamide on cell death reduction. First, D1R over-activation induces cell death-related pathways and D1R-H3R disruption.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that D1R activation leads to cell death and loss of heteromers.

claim: Pre-treatment with H3R ligands can block D1R-induced cell death and prevent D1R-H3R loss.
source: In addition, pre-treatment with H3R ligands can block D1R-induced cell death and prevent D1R-H3R loss.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that thioperamide protects against cell death and preserves heteromers.

claim: The effect of TAT-peptide analogues of D1R transmembrane domains in D1R-H3R stability and function demonstrates specific D1R-H3R, and not D2R-H3R, signaling and function.
source: Finally, the effect of TAT-peptide analogues of D1R transmembrane domains in D1R-H3R stability and function demonstrate that we are observing specific D1R-H3R, and not D2R-H3R, signaling and function.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that D1R TM5 peptide disrupts heteromers and blocks thioperamide's effects.

claim: Thioperamide has been suggested to act via the H4R receptor.
source: Thioperamide has recently been suggested to act via the H4R receptor.
evidence: This is a claim about alternative interpretations in the literature.

claim: H4R is not responsible for the observed effects of thioperamide in this study.
source: However, several pieces of our data suggest H4R is not responsible for the observed effects. First, we measured similar effects using VUF 5681, a different H3R antagonist. In addition we lose all effects of thioperamide in cells where H3R expression was silenced or when D1R-H3R heteromers are lost in the mice yet H4R should still be expressed. Finally, H4R is thought to be mainly expressed peripherally, while our data from brain slices and from mice which are predominatly cognitive in nature, strongly implicate the CNS.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including use of a different H3R antagonist, loss of effect in H3R-depleted cells, and CNS-specific effects.

claim: Growing evidence points to neuronal dysfunction as responsible for the earliest HD disturbances in cognitive and behavioral changes.
source: Besides striatal and cortical cell death, growing evidence points to neuronal dysfunction as responsible for the earliest HD disturbances in cognitive and behavioral changes (Lemiere et al., 2004; Puigdellívol et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Lemiere et al., 2004; Puigdellívol et al., 2016).

claim: No effective treatments are currently available to treat cognitive decline in HD.
source: Despite these early changes, no effective treatments are currently available to treat cognitive decline in HD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the current state of HD treatment.

claim: The timing of intervention is critical since atrophy and dysfunction progress with age and treatment may be different according to the stage of illness.
source: Moreover, the timing of intervention is also critical since atrophy and dysfunction progress with age and treatment may be different according to the stage of illness.
evidence: This is a general principle about disease progression and treatment timing.

claim: Both dopamine and histamine play well-known roles in synaptic plasticity and memory.
source: In this scenario, and given the well-known role of both dopamine and histamine in synaptic plasticity and memory (Cahill et al., 2014; Ellender et al., 2011; Haas et al., 2008; Komater et al., 2005; López de Maturana and Sánchez-Pernaute, 2010; Mohsen et al., 2014; Orsetti et al., 2002; Pascoli et al., 2009; Wiescholleck and Manahan-Vaughan, 2014), it is possible that the therapeutic potential of H3R ligands as modulators of D1R-H3R heteromers could also be extended to improve learning impairments and cognitive decline in HD.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cahill et al., 2014; Ellender et al., 2011; Haas et al., 2008; Komater et al., 2005; López de Maturana and Sánchez-Pernaute, 2010; Mohsen et al., 2014; Orsetti et al., 2002; Pascoli et al., 2009; Wiescholleck and Manahan-Vaughan, 2014).

claim: Chronic treatment with the H3R antagonist thioperamide at 5 months of age prevents motor learning deficits, as well as impaired spatial and recognition memories in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
source: This is supported by our data showing that chronic treatment with the H3R antagonist thioperamide at 5 months of age prevented motor learning deficits, as well as impaired spatial and recognition memories in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from rotarod, NORT, and T-SAT experiments.

claim: Thioperamide treatment does not induce off-target effects (such as alterations in spontaneous locomotor activity or anxiety-like behaviors) in wild-type HdhQ7/Q7 or mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
source: Importantly, thioperamide treatment does not induce off-target effects (such as alterations in spontaneous locomotor activity or anxiety-like behaviors) neither in wild-type HdhQ7/Q7 nor in mutant HdhQ7/Q111 mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by open field behavioral data showing no differences in locomotor activity or anxiety measures.

claim: Early chronic treatment with thioperamide prevents disruption of the heteromer at 6 and 8 months of age and the subsequent cognitive decline.
source: In addition, early chronic treatment with thioperamide prevented disruption of the heteromer at 6 and 8 months of age and the subsequent cognitive decline.
evidence: The claim is supported by PLA data showing preserved heteromers and behavioral data showing preserved cognitive function in thioperamide-treated mice.

claim: There is no direct link between D1R-H3R heteromers and cognitive deficits, but the data suggest that neuronal changes during disease progression are blocked or delayed.
source: It seems unlikely that there is a direct link between D1R-H3R heteromers and cognitive deficits, but the data do suggest that whatever neuronal changes occur during progression of the disease they are blocked or at minimum delayed.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data suggesting indirect effects.

claim: D1R-H3R heteromers are required for the effect of thioperamide on cognitive and motor learning deficits.
source: Importantly, we can say that D1R-H3R heteromers are required for this effect as thioperamide treatment at 7 months of age (when the heteromer is lost in HD mice) is not able to prevent cognitive and motor learning deficits.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that thioperamide is ineffective when treatment starts at 7 months, when heteromers are lost.

claim: GSK189254, an H3R antagonist, showed no change in motor performance and mild improvement in exploratory behavior and cognitive function in a Q175 mouse model of HD.
source: This latter result might explain the results of the effects that GSK189254, an H3R antagonist, have in a Q175 mouse model of HD (Whittaker et al., 2017). The authors saw no change in motor performance and mild improvement in exploratory behavior as measured in the Open Field test and in cognitive function as measured by a T-maze.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Whittaker et al., 2017).

claim: D1R-H3R heteromer expression is crucial to the efficacy of H3R antagonists as a therapeutic option in HD.
source: Our data suggest that D1R-H3R heteromer expression is crucial to the efficacy of H3R antagonists as a therapeutic option in HD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing that thioperamide is only effective when heteromers are present.

claim: Chronic thioperamide treatment at early stages completely rescues the reduction in the density of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta in HD mice in both hippocampal and cortical areas.
source: However, we did find that chronic thioperamide treatment at early stages completely rescue the reduction in the density of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta in HD mice in both hippocampal and cortical areas, suggesting that adequate dopaminergic signaling is required for normal forms of synaptic structural plasticity and cognitive processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by spinophilin immunostaining data.

claim: Adequate dopaminergic signaling is required for normal forms of synaptic structural plasticity and cognitive processes.
source: However, we did find that chronic thioperamide treatment at early stages completely rescue the reduction in the density of spinophilin-immunoreactive puncta in HD mice in both hippocampal and cortical areas, suggesting that adequate dopaminergic signaling is required for normal forms of synaptic structural plasticity and cognitive processes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that thioperamide rescues spinophilin puncta density.

claim: Substantial data support the importance of dopamine receptors for synaptic plasticity in the cortex and hippocampus.
source: Substantial data support the importance of dopamine receptors for synaptic plasticity in the cortex and hippocampus (Levy and Goldman-Rakic, 2000; Robbins, 2000; Sajikumar and Frey, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Levy and Goldman-Rakic, 2000; Robbins, 2000; Sajikumar and Frey, 2004).

claim: Any dopamine imbalance with both suboptimal and supra-optimal dopamine activity has been reported to modify cognitive performance.
source: In this view, any dopamine imbalance with both suboptimal and supra-optimal dopamine activity has been reported to modify cognitive performance (Mattay et al., 2003; Vijayraghavan et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mattay et al., 2003; Vijayraghavan et al., 2007).

claim: The early stages of HD may reflect a hyperdopaminergic stage.
source: As the early stages of HD may reflect a hyperdopaminergic stage (Chen et al., 2013a; Mochel et al., 2011), treatments reducing dopamine signaling may have therapeutic benefits.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chen et al., 2013a; Mochel et al., 2011).

claim: Dopamine-depleting drugs such as tetrabenazine or dopamine-stabilizers as pridopidine show neuroprotective effects in HD mice.
source: In fact, dopamine-depleting drugs such as tetrabenazine or dopamine-stabilizers as pridopidine showed neuroprotective effects in HD mice (Wang et al., 2010), and improve motor coordination abnormalities in HD patients (Huntington Study Group, 2006; de Yebenes et al., 2011), while specific D1R inhibition rescues electrophysiological changes in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission in full-length HD mouse models (André et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Wang et al., 2010; Huntington Study Group, 2006; de Yebenes et al., 2011; André et al., 2011b).

claim: The concept of heteromers has been known for over a decade but physiologic examples have only recently come to be appreciated.
source: The concept of heteromers have been known for over a decade but physiologic examples have only recently come to be appreciated (Bonaventura et al., 2015; Viñals et al., 2015; Baba et al., 2013; Fribourg et al., 2011; González et al., 2012a González et al., 2012b; Kern et al., 2012; Navarro et al., 2015).

claim: H3R antagonists can prevent learning and memory deficits by blocking D1R in D1R-H3R complexes.
source: In sum, our study showing that H3R antagonists can prevent learning and memory deficits by blocking D1R in D1R-H3R complexes, along with the role of these heteromers on neuronal cell death, predict a critical role of the histaminergic system as modulator of the dopamine imbalance in HD, and may help to overcome the deleterious effects of directly manipulating DA-production and/or signaling, thus opening new and important alternatives for HD therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.
